content.text: Turning categories into 1, 2, 3 hands the model an order and distances that don't exist. A linear model then has to fit one slope across arbitrary codes, and in the example below it barely beats guessing the average. One-hot encode unordered categories, use native categorical support in gradient-boosted trees, and keep integer codes for categories that really have an order.
A delivery app wants to predict how long an order takes. The data has a

column, so someone maps each city to an integer, Alexandria = 0 through Luxor = 4, and fits a linear regression. The mean absolute error comes out at 9.7 minutes; a model that always predicts the average is off by 9.8. The team concludes that linear models are too weak for the job and reaches for something bigger. The model wasn't the problem. The column was.
Many developers map each category to an integer and move on. It looks reasonable for good reasons:

items.text: Models need numbers, and one integer per category is the smallest encoding there is: one column in, one column out.
. Plenty of tutorials do exactly that.
With tree-based models it often seems to work, and scikit-learn's own gradient boosting example says ordinal codes may work well for features with few categories.
In application code an integer ID is harmless. Nobody adds two
values, so the number feels like a label.

content.text: The half-truth: an integer is a perfectly good
for a category. The problem is that a model doesn't read it as a name. It reads a quantity.
To a model, every feature is a number on a scale, and the encoding decides what that scale says.
A code brings an order and a distance

With Alexandria = 0, Aswan = 1, Cairo = 2, Giza = 3 and Luxor = 4, the data now claims that Cairo sits between Aswan and Giza, that Luxor is twice Cairo, and that Alexandria is as far from Aswan as Giza is from Luxor. None of it is true; the order is just the alphabet. The scikit-learn user guide says it directly: estimators expect continuous input, so they would interpret integer-coded categories as ordered, which is often not what you want. Google's Machine Learning Crash Course makes the same point with colors: stored as index numbers, they're treated as floating-point values, and purple becomes six times orange.
One weight can't describe five cities
A linear model learns one weight per column. With a single

column, that weight is a slope: each step along the codes adds the same number of minutes. In the script below, the five cities average 30, 55, 25, 45 and 35 minutes, in alphabetical order. No straight line fits that zigzag.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
avg = {"Alexandria": 30, "Aswan": 55, "Cairo": 25, "Giza": 45, "Luxor": 35}
city = pd.DataFrame({"city": rng.choice(list(avg), size=1000)})
minutes = city["city"].map(avg) + rng.normal(0, 5, size=1000)

X = OrdinalEncoder().fit_transform(city)  # Alexandria=0, Aswan=1 ... Luxor=4
slope = LinearRegression().fit(X, minutes).coef_[0]
print(f"{slope:+.2f} min per step along the alphabet")  # +0.34
for model in [LinearRegression(), DummyRegressor()]:  # Dummy: always the mean
    mae = -cross_val_score(model, X, minutes, cv=5,
                           scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()
    print(f"{type(model).__name__:<16} MAE {mae:.1f} min")
# LinearRegression MAE 9.7 min
# DummyRegressor   MAE 9.8 min

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
avg = {"Alexandria": 30, "Aswan": 55, "Cairo": 25, "Giza": 45, "Luxor": 35}
city = pd.DataFrame({"city": rng.choice(list(avg), size=1000)})
minutes = city["city"].map(avg) + rng.normal(0, 5, size=1000)

one_hot = make_pipeline(OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"),
                        LinearRegression())  # one weight per city
native = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(categorical_features="from_dtype")
for name, model, X in [("one-hot + linear", one_hot, city),
                       ("native categories", native, city.astype("category"))]:
    mae = -cross_val_score(model, X, minutes, cv=5,
                           scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()
    print(f"{name:<17} MAE {mae:.1f} min")
# one-hot + linear  MAE 3.9 min
# native categories MAE 3.9 min

content.text: The slope comes out at +0.34 minutes per step: the model learned that cities later in the alphabet are slightly slower, which means nothing. Its cross-validated error, 9.7 minutes, is barely better than the 9.8 of
that always predicts the average. The information is in the data; the encoding hid it.

gives each category its own column, set to 1 for that category and 0 for all the others. Five cities become five columns, and the linear model learns five independent weights with no order between them. The same
drops to 3.9 minutes, close to the floor set by the random noise in the data. The model didn't change;

A decision tree splits on thresholds, so it can cut one city out of the codes with two splits. That's why integer codes often look fine with tree models. scikit-learn's gradient boosting example on the Ames housing data agrees that ordinal codes may work for low-cardinality features, but notes that meaningful splits need deeper trees as the number of categories grows. Its illustration: if the best way to split categories A to F is ACF against BDE, ordinal codes need 4 splits, one-hot needs 3, and native categorical handling needs 1.
has that native support. It treats pandas

columns as unordered groups, the default behavior since scikit-learn 1.6, and in the script it matches one-hot at 3.9 minutes with no encoder at all. Each such feature can have at most 255 categories.

One-hot has its own limit. The Crash Course calls it usually a bad choice when the number of categories is high, such as roughly 42,000 US postal codes, and suggests embeddings instead. In scikit-learn you can merge rare categories into one column with
, which the user guide recommends for high-cardinality features like zip codes. It replaces each category with a smoothed average of the target; call
on training data, which cross-fits so a row's own target doesn't leak into its encoding.

items.text: An integer code tells the model that categories are ordered and evenly spaced, even when the order is the alphabet.
On codes, a linear model fits one slope across arbitrary categories: 9.7 minutes of error, against 9.8 for guessing the average and 3.9 with one-hot encoding.
Trees tolerate codes but need extra splits; gradient boosting's native categorical support avoids them.
Use integer codes only for categories with a real order, and pass that order explicitly.
